claim: Virophages can parasitize giant DNA viruses.
source: Virophages can parasitize giant DNA viruses and may provide adaptive anti-giant virus defense in unicellular eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Virophages may provide adaptive anti-giant virus defense in unicellular eukaryotes.
source: Virophages can parasitize giant DNA viruses and may provide adaptive anti-giant virus defense in unicellular eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of virophages.

claim: Under laboratory conditions, the virophage mavirus integrates into the nuclear genome of the marine flagellate Cafeteria burkhardae.
source: Under laboratory conditions, the virophage mavirus integrates into the nuclear genome of the marine flagellate Cafeteria burkhardae and reactivates upon superinfection with the giant virus CroV.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior experimental work cited in the manuscript (Fischer and Hackl, 2016).

claim: Mavirus reactivates upon superinfection with the giant virus CroV.
source: Under laboratory conditions, the virophage mavirus integrates into the nuclear genome of the marine flagellate Cafeteria burkhardae and reactivates upon superinfection with the giant virus CroV.
evidence: This is supported by prior experimental work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Four globally sampled C. burkhardae strains contain dozens of integrated virophages.
source: Here, we report dozens of integrated virophages in four globally sampled C. burkhardae strains that constitute up to 2% of their host genomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Integrated virophages constitute up to 2% of C. burkhardae host genomes.
source: Here, we report dozens of integrated virophages in four globally sampled C. burkhardae strains that constitute up to 2% of their host genomes.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative genomic analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Endogenous mavirus-like elements (EMALEs) separated into eight types based on GC-content, nucleotide similarity, and coding potential.
source: These endogenous mavirus-like elements (EMALEs) separated into eight types based on GC-content, nucleotide similarity, and coding potential and carried diverse promoter motifs implicating interactions with different giant viruses.
evidence: This classification is supported by dot plot analysis (Figure 2) and phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4).

claim: EMALEs carried diverse promoter motifs implicating interactions with different giant viruses.
source: These endogenous mavirus-like elements (EMALEs) separated into eight types based on GC-content, nucleotide similarity, and coding potential and carried diverse promoter motifs implicating interactions with different giant viruses.
evidence: This is supported by promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Some EMALE insertion loci were conserved between host strains indicating ancient integration events.
source: Between host strains, some EMALE insertion loci were conserved indicating ancient integration events, whereas the majority of insertion sites were unique to a given host strain suggesting that EMALEs are active and mobile.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis of EMALE insertion sites across strains.

claim: The majority of EMALE insertion sites were unique to a given host strain suggesting that EMALEs are active and mobile.
source: Between host strains, some EMALE insertion loci were conserved indicating ancient integration events, whereas the majority of insertion sites were unique to a given host strain suggesting that EMALEs are active and mobile.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis and is an inference about EMALE activity.

claim: A unique association exists between EMALEs and a group of tyrosine recombinase retrotransposons.
source: Furthermore, we uncovered a unique association between EMALEs and a group of tyrosine recombinase retrotransposons, revealing yet another layer of parasitism in this nested microbial system.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data showing Ngaro retrotransposon insertions in EMALEs (Figure 5).

claim: The association between EMALEs and tyrosine recombinase retrotransposons reveals another layer of parasitism in this nested microbial system.
source: Furthermore, we uncovered a unique association between EMALEs and a group of tyrosine recombinase retrotransposons, revealing yet another layer of parasitism in this nested microbial system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed association between EMALEs and Ngaro elements.

claim: Virophages are widespread in wild Cafeteria populations.
source: Our findings show that virophages are widespread and dynamic in wild Cafeteria populations, supporting their potential role in antiviral defense in protists.
evidence: This is supported by the discovery of numerous EMALEs in four globally sampled strains.

claim: Virophages are dynamic in wild Cafeteria populations.
source: Our findings show that virophages are widespread and dynamic in wild Cafeteria populations, supporting their potential role in antiviral defense in protists.
evidence: This is inferred from the variability of EMALE insertion sites among strains.

claim: The findings support the potential role of virophages in antiviral defense in protists.
source: Our findings show that virophages are widespread and dynamic in wild Cafeteria populations, supporting their potential role in antiviral defense in protists.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Many eukaryotic genomes harbor endogenous viral elements (EVEs).
source: Many eukaryotic genomes harbor endogenous viral elements (EVEs) (Feschotte and Gilbert, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: For retroviruses, integration as a provirus is an essential part of their replication cycles.
source: For retroviruses, integration as a provirus is an essential part of their replication cycles, but other viruses also occasionally endogenize, for instance with the help of cellular retroelements (Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Other viruses also occasionally endogenize, for instance with the help of cellular retroelements.
source: For retroviruses, integration as a provirus is an essential part of their replication cycles, but other viruses also occasionally endogenize, for instance with the help of cellular retroelements (Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Some green algal genomes contain giant EVEs of several hundred kilobase pairs in length.
source: Some green algal genomes even contain giant EVEs of several hundred kilobase pairs (kbp) in length (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020), but unlike prophages in bacteria and archaea, most eukaryotic EVEs are thought to be 'genomic fossils' and incapable of virion formation and horizontal transmission.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Most eukaryotic EVEs are thought to be 'genomic fossils' and incapable of virion formation and horizontal transmission.
source: Some green algal genomes even contain giant EVEs of several hundred kilobase pairs (kbp) in length (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020), but unlike prophages in bacteria and archaea, most eukaryotic EVEs are thought to be 'genomic fossils' and incapable of virion formation and horizontal transmission.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some viral genes may be co-opted for various host functions.
source: However, some viral genes may be co-opted for various host functions (Frank and Feschotte, 2017; Aswad and Katzourakis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Viruses of the family Lavidaviridae depend for their replication on giant DNA viruses of the family Mimiviridae.
source: Viruses of the family Lavidaviridae, commonly known as virophages, depend for their replication on giant DNA viruses of the family Mimiviridae and can parasitize them during coinfection of a suitable protist host (La Scola et al., 2008; Krupovic et al., 2016a; Duponchel and Fischer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Virophages can parasitize giant DNA viruses during coinfection of a suitable protist host.
source: Viruses of the family Lavidaviridae, commonly known as virophages, depend for their replication on giant DNA viruses of the family Mimiviridae and can parasitize them during coinfection of a suitable protist host (La Scola et al., 2008; Krupovic et al., 2016a; Duponchel and Fischer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The virophage mavirus strongly inhibits virion synthesis of the lytic giant virus CroV during coinfection of the marine heterotrophic nanoflagellate Cafeteria sp.
source: A striking example is the virophage mavirus, which strongly inhibits virion synthesis of the lytic giant virus CroV during coinfection of the marine heterotrophic nanoflagellate Cafeteria sp. (Stramenopiles; Bicosoecida) (Fischer and Suttle, 2011; Fischer and Hackl, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Virophages possess 15–30 kbp long double-stranded (ds) DNA genomes of circular or linear topology.
source: Virophages possess 15–30 kbp long double-stranded (ds) DNA genomes of circular or linear topology that tend to have low GC-contents (27–51%) (Fischer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Virophage genomes tend to have low GC-contents (27–51%).
source: Virophages possess 15–30 kbp long double-stranded (ds) DNA genomes of circular or linear topology that tend to have low GC-contents (27–51%) (Fischer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A typical virophage genome encodes 20–30 proteins.
source: A typical virophage genome encodes 20–30 proteins, including a major capsid protein (MCP), a minor capsid or penton protein (PEN), a DNA packaging ATPase, and a maturation cysteine protease (PRO) (Krupovic et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Virophages encode DNA replication and integration proteins that were likely acquired independently in different virophage lineages.
source: In addition to this conserved morphogenesis module, virophages encode DNA replication and integration proteins that were likely acquired independently in different virophage lineages (Yutin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Viruses in the genus Mavirus contain a rve-family integrase (rve-INT) that is also found in retrotransposons and retroviruses.
source: Viruses in the genus Mavirus contain a rve-family integrase (rve-INT) that is also found in retrotransposons and retroviruses, with close homologs among the eukaryotic Maverick/Polinton elements (MPEs) (Fischer and Suttle, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: MPEs were initially described as DNA transposons.
source: MPEs were initially described as DNA transposons (Pritham et al., 2007; Kapitonov and Jurka, 2006), but many of them carry the morphogenesis gene module and thus qualify as endogenous viruses (Krupovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many MPEs carry the morphogenesis gene module and thus qualify as endogenous viruses.
source: MPEs were initially described as DNA transposons (Pritham et al., 2007; Kapitonov and Jurka, 2006), but many of them carry the morphogenesis gene module and thus qualify as endogenous viruses (Krupovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis suggests that mavirus-type virophages share a common ancestry with MPEs and the related Polinton-like viruses (PLVs).
source: Phylogenetic analysis suggests that mavirus-type virophages share a common ancestry with MPEs and the related Polinton-like viruses (PLVs) (Fischer and Suttle, 2011; Yutin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mavirus integrates efficiently into the nuclear host genome.
source: We therefore tested the integration capacity of mavirus using the cultured protist Cafeteria burkhardae (formerly Cafeteria roenbergensis; Fenchel and Patterson, 1988; Schoenle et al., 2020) and found that mavirus integrates efficiently into the nuclear host genome (Fischer and Hackl, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Mavirus provirophages are transcriptionally silent unless the host cell is infected with CroV.
source: The resulting mavirus provirophages are transcriptionally silent unless the host cell is infected with CroV, which leads to reactivation and virion formation of mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work (Fischer and Hackl, 2016).

claim: CroV infection leads to reactivation and virion formation of mavirus.
source: The resulting mavirus provirophages are transcriptionally silent unless the host cell is infected with CroV, which leads to reactivation and virion formation of mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Newly produced virophage particles inhibit CroV replication and increase host population survival during subsequent rounds of coinfection.
source: Newly produced virophage particles then inhibit CroV replication and increase host population survival during subsequent rounds of coinfection (Fischer and Hackl, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The mutualistic Cafeteria-mavirus symbiosis may act as an adaptive defense system against lytic giant viruses.
source: The mutualistic Cafeteria-mavirus symbiosis may thus act as an adaptive defense system against lytic giant viruses (Fischer and Hackl, 2016; Koonin and Krupovic, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The integrated state of mavirus represents the host's indirect antigenic memory of CroV.
source: The integrated state of mavirus is pivotal to the proposed defense scheme as it represents the host's indirect antigenic memory of CroV (Koonin and Krupovic, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Mavirus-like EVEs are common, diverse, and most likely active mobile genetic elements (MGEs) of C. burkhardae.
source: Here, we report that mavirus-like EVEs are common, diverse, and most likely active mobile genetic elements (MGEs) of C. burkhardae.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the genomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: High-quality de novo genome assemblies of four cultured C. burkhardae strains were generated.
source: In preparation of screening for endogenous virophages, we generated high-quality de novo genome assemblies of four cultured C. burkhardae strains (Hackl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and methods described in the manuscript.

claim: C. burkhardae strain BVI was isolated from the Caribbean Sea in 2012.
source: These strains, designated BVI, Cflag, E4-10P (E4-10), and RCC970-E3 (RCC970), were isolated from the Caribbean Sea in 2012, the Northwest Atlantic in 1986, the Northeast Pacific in 1989, and the Southeast Pacific in 2004, respectively.
evidence: This is factual information about strain isolation.

claim: C. burkhardae strain Cflag was isolated from the Northwest Atlantic in 1986.
source: These strains, designated BVI, Cflag, E4-10P (E4-10), and RCC970-E3 (RCC970), were isolated from the Caribbean Sea in 2012, the Northwest Atlantic in 1986, the Northeast Pacific in 1989, and the Southeast Pacific in 2004, respectively.
evidence: This is factual information about strain isolation.

claim: C. burkhardae strain E4-10 was isolated from the Northeast Pacific in 1989.
source: These strains, designated BVI, Cflag, E4-10P (E4-10), and RCC970-E3 (RCC970), were isolated from the Caribbean Sea in 2012, the Northwest Atlantic in 1986, the Northeast Pacific in 1989, and the Southeast Pacific in 2004, respectively.
evidence: This is factual information about strain isolation.

claim: C. burkhardae strain RCC970 was isolated from the Southeast Pacific in 2004.
source: These strains, designated BVI, Cflag, E4-10P (E4-10), and RCC970-E3 (RCC970), were isolated from the Caribbean Sea in 2012, the Northwest Atlantic in 1986, the Northeast Pacific in 1989, and the Southeast Pacific in 2004, respectively.
evidence: This is factual information about strain isolation.

claim: The genomes were sequenced using both short-read (Illumina MiSeq) and long-read (Pacific Biosciences RSII) technologies.
source: We sequenced their genomes using both short-read (Illumina MiSeq) and long-read (Pacific Biosciences RSII) technologies in order to produce assemblies that would resolve 20–30 kb long repetitive elements within the host genomic context.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: Each C. burkhardae genome assembly comprised of 34–36 megabase pairs with an average GC-content of 70%.
source: Each C. burkhardae genome assembly comprised of 34–36 megabase pairs with an average GC-content of 70% (Hackl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and citation.

claim: Endogenous virophages were identified by combining sequence similarity searches against known virophage genomes with genomic screening for GC-content anomalies.
source: To identify endogenous virophages, we combined sequence similarity searches against known virophage genomes with genomic screening for GC-content anomalies.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: Virophage elements were clearly discernible from eukaryotic genome regions based on their low (30–50%) GC-content.
source: The two approaches yielded redundant results and virophage elements were clearly discernible from eukaryotic genome regions based on their low (30–50%) GC-content (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each virophage element had at least one open reading frame (ORF) with a top blastp hit to a mavirus protein.
source: Each element had at least one open reading frame (ORF) with a top blastp hit to a mavirus protein, with no elements bearing close resemblance to Sputnik or other virophages outside the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by sequence similarity analysis.

claim: No elements bore close resemblance to Sputnik or other virophages outside the genus Mavirus.
source: Each element had at least one open reading frame (ORF) with a top blastp hit to a mavirus protein, with no elements bearing close resemblance to Sputnik or other virophages outside the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by sequence similarity analysis.

claim: In the four Cafeteria genomes combined, 138 endogenous mavirus-like elements (EMALEs) were found.
source: In the four Cafeteria genomes combined, we found 138 endogenous mavirus-like elements (EMALEs, Figure 1B and C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data shown in figures.

claim: Thirty-three EMALEs were flanked by terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) and host DNA and can be considered full-length viral genomes.
source: Thirty-three of these elements were flanked by terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) and host DNA and can thus be considered full-length viral genomes.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis of EMALE structure.

claim: C. burkhardae strain BVI contained 55 EMALEs, nearly twice as many as any of the other strains.
source: With 55 elements, C. burkhardae strain BVI contained nearly twice as many EMALEs as any of the other strains, where we found 27–29 elements per genome (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Strains Cflag, E4-10, and RCC970 contained 27–29 EMALEs per genome.
source: With 55 elements, C. burkhardae strain BVI contained nearly twice as many EMALEs as any of the other strains, where we found 27–29 elements per genome (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EMALEs composed an estimated 0.7–1.8% of each host assembly.
source: Compared to the total assembly length, EMALEs composed an estimated 0.7–1.8% of each host assembly (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Contributions calculated from assemblies deviated only slightly (0.01–0.3%) from read-based calculations.
source: Contributions calculated from assemblies deviated only slightly (0.01–0.3%) from read-based calculations.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of assembly-based and read-based quantification.

claim: The assemblies provide a good representation of the actual contribution of EMALEs to the overall host genomes.
source: Therefore, the assemblies seem to provide a good representation of the actual contribution of EMALEs to the overall host genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of assembly-based and read-based calculations.

claim: The 33 complete EMALE genomes were 5.5–21.5 kb long with a median length of 19.8 kb.
source: From here on, we focus our analysis on the 33 complete EMALE genomes, which were 5.5–21.5 kb long with a median length of 19.8 kb, and TIRs that varied in length from 0.2 to 2.3 kb with a median of 0.9 kb (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: EMALE TIRs varied in length from 0.2 to 2.3 kb with a median of 0.9 kb.
source: From here on, we focus our analysis on the 33 complete EMALE genomes, which were 5.5–21.5 kb long with a median length of 19.8 kb, and TIRs that varied in length from 0.2 to 2.3 kb with a median of 0.9 kb (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: EMALE GC-contents ranged from 29.7% to 52.7%, excluding retrotransposon insertions.
source: Their GC-contents ranged from 29.7% to 52.7%, excluding retrotransposon insertions where present.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: An all-versus-all DNA dot plot approach revealed two main blocks of EMALEs.
source: To classify EMALEs we used an all-versus-all DNA dot plot approach (Figure 2). It revealed two main blocks: The first block contained EMALEs with GC-contents of 29.7–38.5% (median 35.3%), whereas EMALEs in the second block had GC-contents ranging from 47.2% to 52.7% (median 49.3%).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first block of EMALEs contained elements with GC-contents of 29.7–38.5% (median 35.3%).
source: To classify EMALEs we used an all-versus-all DNA dot plot approach (Figure 2). It revealed two main blocks: The first block contained EMALEs with GC-contents of 29.7–38.5% (median 35.3%), whereas EMALEs in the second block had GC-contents ranging from 47.2% to 52.7% (median 49.3%).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second block of EMALEs had GC-contents ranging from 47.2% to 52.7% (median 49.3%).
source: To classify EMALEs we used an all-versus-all DNA dot plot approach (Figure 2). It revealed two main blocks: The first block contained EMALEs with GC-contents of 29.7–38.5% (median 35.3%), whereas EMALEs in the second block had GC-contents ranging from 47.2% to 52.7% (median 49.3%).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: C. burkhardae EMALEs can be separated into low-GC and mid-GC groups.
source: The C. burkhardae EMALEs can thus be roughly separated into low-GC and mid-GC groups.
evidence: This is inferred from the GC-content analysis.

claim: Low-GC EMALEs comprise types 1–4.
source: Based on the similarity patterns within each block, we further distinguish eight EMALE types, with low-GC EMALEs comprising types 1–4 and mid-GC EMALEs comprising types 5–8 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mid-GC EMALEs comprise types 5–8.
source: Based on the similarity patterns within each block, we further distinguish eight EMALE types, with low-GC EMALEs comprising types 1–4 and mid-GC EMALEs comprising types 5–8 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reference mavirus strain Spezl falls within type 4 of the low-GC EMALEs.
source: According to this classification scheme, the reference mavirus strain Spezl falls within type 4 of the low-GC EMALEs (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The codon and amino acid composition of EMALE genes clearly correlated with the overall GC-content of the EMALE genomes.
source: The codon and amino acid composition of EMALE genes clearly correlated with the overall GC-content of the EMALE genomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by codon usage analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For each encoded amino acid, there was a strong shift toward synonymous codons reflecting the overall GC trend.
source: For each encoded amino acid, we observed a strong shift toward synonymous codons reflecting the overall GC trend, and across amino acids, we observed a shift from those encoded by high-GC codons to those encoded by low-GC codons in low-GC EMALEs and vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by codon usage analysis.

claim: Selection and evolutionary processes driving GC-content variation in virophages likely act on the nucleotide level, rather than on the encoded proteins.
source: This uniform trend across all amino acids likely indicates that selection and evolutionary processes driving GC-content variation in these viruses act on the nucleotide level, rather than on the encoded proteins.
evidence: This is an inference from the codon usage analysis.

claim: EMALEs are predicted to encode 17–21 proteins each, with few exceptions.
source: With few exceptions, EMALEs are predicted to encode 17–21 proteins each.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation data.

claim: None of the EMALE encoding genes was found to contain introns.
source: None of the encoding genes was found to contain introns.
evidence: This is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: The virion morphogenesis module in EMALE types 1 and 3–7 consists of the canonical virophage core genes corresponding to MCP, PEN, ATPase, and PRO proteins.
source: The virion morphogenesis module in EMALE types 1 and 3–7 consists of the canonical virophage core genes corresponding to MCP, PEN, ATPase, and PRO proteins.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and comparison to known virophage genes.

claim: Type 2 EMALEs likely encode a different set of capsid genes.
source: Type 2 EMALEs likely encode a different set of capsid genes as discussed below, and the truncated EMALE type 8 lacks recognizable morphogenesis genes.
evidence: This is inferred from gene annotation and comparison.

claim: The truncated EMALE type 8 lacks recognizable morphogenesis genes.
source: Type 2 EMALEs likely encode a different set of capsid genes as discussed below, and the truncated EMALE type 8 lacks recognizable morphogenesis genes.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: MV14 is a highly conserved gene in EMALE types 1 and 3–7.
source: Another highly conserved gene in EMALE types 1 and 3–7 is MV14, which is always found immediately upstream of the ATPase (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and codes for a protein of unknown function that is part of the mavirus virion (Born et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and citation.

claim: MV14 is always found immediately upstream of the ATPase.
source: Another highly conserved gene in EMALE types 1 and 3–7 is MV14, which is always found immediately upstream of the ATPase (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and codes for a protein of unknown function that is part of the mavirus virion (Born et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis shown in figures.

claim: MV14 codes for a protein of unknown function that is part of the mavirus virion.
source: Another highly conserved gene in EMALE types 1 and 3–7 is MV14, which is always found immediately upstream of the ATPase (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and codes for a protein of unknown function that is part of the mavirus virion (Born et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MV14 is present in various metagenomic virophage sequences.
source: MV14 is present in various metagenomic virophage sequences (Paez-Espino et al., 2019) and, based on synteny and protein localization, likely encodes an important virion component in members of the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MV14 likely encodes an important virion component in members of the genus Mavirus.
source: MV14 is present in various metagenomic virophage sequences (Paez-Espino et al., 2019) and, based on synteny and protein localization, likely encodes an important virion component in members of the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is inferred from synteny and protein localization data.

claim: The replication/integration module consists of the rve-INT gene and at least one additional ORF coding for a primase/helicase and a DNA polymerase.
source: The replication/integration module consists of the rve-INT gene and at least one additional ORF coding for a primase/helicase and a DNA polymerase.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: Low-GC EMALEs encode a mavirus-related primase/helicase and protein-primed family B DNA polymerase (pPolB).
source: Low-GC EMALEs encode a mavirus-related primase/helicase and protein-primed family B DNA polymerase (pPolB) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation shown in figures.

claim: Mid-GC EMALEs lack the pPolB gene.
source: Mid-GC EMALEs, on the other hand, lack the pPolB gene and feature a longer primase/helicase ORF that may include a DNA polymerase domain similar to the helicase-polymerase fusion genes described in PLVs (Krupovic et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: Mid-GC EMALEs feature a longer primase/helicase ORF that may include a DNA polymerase domain similar to the helicase-polymerase fusion genes described in PLVs.
source: Mid-GC EMALEs, on the other hand, lack the pPolB gene and feature a longer primase/helicase ORF that may include a DNA polymerase domain similar to the helicase-polymerase fusion genes described in PLVs (Krupovic et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is inferred from gene annotation and comparison to PLVs, supported by citation.

claim: Other mavirus genes frequently found in EMALEs include MV19, MV08, and MV12.
source: Other mavirus genes frequently found in EMALEs include MV19 (encoding a putative protease domain), and two genes of unknown function, MV08 and MV12.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: All mid-GC EMALEs encode a predicted tyrosine recombinase (YR) in addition to the rve-INT.
source: Interestingly, all mid-GC EMALEs encode a predicted tyrosine recombinase (YR) in addition to the rve-INT and thus possess two predicted enzymes for genome integration.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: Mid-GC EMALEs possess two predicted enzymes for genome integration.
source: Interestingly, all mid-GC EMALEs encode a predicted tyrosine recombinase (YR) in addition to the rve-INT and thus possess two predicted enzymes for genome integration.
evidence: This is inferred from gene annotation.

claim: YRs have been found in other virophages and likely catalyze integration into giant virus genomes.
source: YRs have been found in other virophages and likely catalyze integration into giant virus genomes (Desnues et al., 2012; Yutin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EMALE07 encodes a putative DNA methylase and a ribonucleotide reductase small subunit gene.
source: Notable genes unique to one EMALE type include a putative DNA methylase and a ribonucleotide reductase small subunit gene found in EMALE07.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: The Tlr6F protein encoded by EMALE types 1 + 2 is present in diverse MGEs.
source: The Tlr6F protein encoded by EMALE types 1 + 2 is present in diverse MGEs, including other virophages, PLVs, and large DNA viruses of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota (Koonin and Krupovic, 2017; Stough et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type.
source: In general, genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type, whereas gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types, with the following exceptions: MCP was always preceded by PEN, and ATPase was always preceded by MV14, whereas the MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis.

claim: Gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types.
source: In general, genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type, whereas gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types, with the following exceptions: MCP was always preceded by PEN, and ATPase was always preceded by MV14, whereas the MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis.

claim: MCP was always preceded by PEN in EMALEs.
source: In general, genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type, whereas gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types, with the following exceptions: MCP was always preceded by PEN, and ATPase was always preceded by MV14, whereas the MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis.

claim: ATPase was always preceded by MV14 in EMALEs.
source: In general, genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type, whereas gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types, with the following exceptions: MCP was always preceded by PEN, and ATPase was always preceded by MV14, whereas the MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis.

claim: The MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
source: In general, genes were syntenic between EMALEs of the same type, whereas gene order was poorly conserved among EMALEs of different types, with the following exceptions: MCP was always preceded by PEN, and ATPase was always preceded by MV14, whereas the MV14-ATPase-PRO-PEN-MCP morphogenesis gene order as seen in mavirus was present only in EMALE types 4–7.
evidence: This is supported by gene synteny analysis.

claim: EMALE02 shares 6–7 kb of its 5' part with EMALE01.
source: EMALE02 represents an interesting case, as it shares 6–7 kb of its 5' part (we chose the primase/helicase genes to mark the 5' end of all EMALEs) with EMALE01, while the remaining 11 kb are not closely related to other EMALEs or virophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The remaining 11 kb of EMALE02 are not closely related to other EMALEs or virophages.
source: EMALE02 represents an interesting case, as it shares 6–7 kb of its 5' part (we chose the primase/helicase genes to mark the 5' end of all EMALEs) with EMALE01, while the remaining 11 kb are not closely related to other EMALEs or virophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: EMALE02 may be the result of a recombination event that exchanged the canonical virophage morphogenesis module of EMALE01 with capsid genes of a PLV.
source: EMALE02 may thus be the result of a recombination event that exchanged the canonical virophage morphogenesis module of EMALE01 with capsid genes of a PLV (Figure 3, dashed line).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: Recombination and non-homologous gene replacement are important factors in virophage genome evolution.
source: Overall, these observations support the notion that recombination and non-homologous gene replacement are important factors in virophage genome evolution (Yutin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observations and supported by citation.

claim: EMALE core proteins formed monophyletic clades with mavirus and related sequences from environmental samples.
source: In the resulting phylogenetic trees, EMALE core proteins formed monophyletic clades with mavirus and related sequences from environmental samples, thus significantly expanding the known diversity of the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: EMALEs significantly expand the known diversity of the genus Mavirus.
source: In the resulting phylogenetic trees, EMALE core proteins formed monophyletic clades with mavirus and related sequences from environmental samples, thus significantly expanding the known diversity of the genus Mavirus.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The environmental sequences that clustered with EMALE core proteins include a single amplified genome (SAG) from an uncultured chrysophyte.
source: The environmental sequences that clustered with EMALE core proteins include a single amplified genome (SAG) from an uncultured chrysophyte (Castillo et al., 2019), the metagenomic Ace Lake Mavirus (ALM) (Zhou et al., 2013), and four additional metagenomes that were identified in a global survey of virophage sequences (Paez-Espino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations.

claim: The chrysophyte SAG is nearly identical to mavirus strain Spezl.
source: The chrysophyte SAG is nearly identical to mavirus strain Spezl and indicates that the host range of mavirus extends beyond bicosoecids.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison.

claim: The host range of mavirus extends beyond bicosoecids.
source: The chrysophyte SAG is nearly identical to mavirus strain Spezl and indicates that the host range of mavirus extends beyond bicosoecids.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of mavirus-like sequences in a chrysophyte.

claim: EMALEs of a given type were monophyletic for each of the four core proteins.
source: Within the Mavirus clade, EMALEs of a given type were monophyletic for each of the four core proteins, which corroborates their dot plot-based classification.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The monophyly of EMALE types corroborates their dot plot-based classification.
source: Within the Mavirus clade, EMALEs of a given type were monophyletic for each of the four core proteins, which corroborates their dot plot-based classification.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between phylogenetic and dot plot analyses.

claim: EMALEs of types 5 and 6 are largely syntenic but were clearly distinguishable in their phylogenetic signatures.
source: It is worth noting that although EMALEs of types 5 and 6 are largely syntenic (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), they were clearly distinguishable in their phylogenetic signatures (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and synteny analyses.

claim: Individual core proteins differed with regard to their neighboring clades in phylogenetic trees.
source: A comparison of clade topologies revealed that even within the conserved morphogenesis module, individual proteins differed with regard to their neighboring clades, and low-GC and mid-GC EMALEs did not cluster separately from each other.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of phylogenetic trees.

claim: Low-GC and mid-GC EMALEs did not cluster separately from each other in core protein phylogenies.
source: A comparison of clade topologies revealed that even within the conserved morphogenesis module, individual proteins differed with regard to their neighboring clades, and low-GC and mid-GC EMALEs did not cluster separately from each other.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The morphogenesis modules of different EMALE types may have diversified simultaneously.
source: These observations could suggest that the morphogenesis modules of different EMALE types diversified simultaneously and that adaptation of GC-content may occur rather quickly.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Adaptation of GC-content may occur rather quickly in EMALEs.
source: These observations could suggest that the morphogenesis modules of different EMALE types diversified simultaneously and that adaptation of GC-content may occur rather quickly.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of rve-INT proteins revealed separate clades for low-GC and mid-GC EMALEs.
source: In contrast, phylogenetic analysis of rve-INT proteins revealed separate clades for low-GC and mid-GC EMALEs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each rve-INT clade was affiliated with different cellular homologs that included MPEs and retroelements.
source: Each of these clades was affiliated with different cellular homologs that included MPEs and retroelements.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The rve-INT genes of low-GC EMALEs were located near the 5' end of the genomes.
source: Notably, the rve-INT genes of low-GC EMALEs were located near the 5' end of the genomes, whereas in mid-GC EMALEs, they were located near the 3' end (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene position analysis shown in figures.

claim: In mid-GC EMALEs, rve-INT genes were located near the 3' end.
source: Notably, the rve-INT genes of low-GC EMALEs were located near the 5' end of the genomes, whereas in mid-GC EMALEs, they were located near the 3' end (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene position analysis shown in figures.

claim: EMALEs encode two different rve-INT versions.
source: These observations suggest that EMALEs encode two different rve-INT versions, one specific for low-GC EMALEs that co-occurs with the pPolB and a shorter primase/helicase ORF, and one specific for mid-GC EMALEs that co-occurs with a longer primase/helicase ORF.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic and gene organization analyses.

claim: The two integrase versions may have been acquired independently, or one version could have replaced the other during EMALE evolution.
source: The two integrase versions may have been acquired independently, or one version could have replaced the other during EMALE evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Non-homologous gene replacement appears to have taken place among the primase/helicase genes.
source: Such non-homologous gene replacement appears to have taken place among the primase/helicase genes, too, as previously noted for virophages in general (Yutin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence divergence and supported by citation.

claim: EMALEs encode several different versions of primase/helicase genes with a degree of amino acid divergence that precluded their inclusion in a single multiple sequence alignment.
source: EMALEs encode several different versions of primase/helicase genes with a degree of amino acid divergence that precluded their inclusion in a single multiple sequence alignment.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The YR proteins encoded by EMALE types 5–8 formed a monophyletic clade.
source: The YR proteins encoded by EMALE types 5–8 formed a monophyletic clade and were part of a larger group of recombinases that included virophages from freshwater metagenomes, as well as microalgae and algal nucleocytoviruses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EMALE YR proteins were part of a larger group of recombinases that included virophages from freshwater metagenomes, as well as microalgae and algal nucleocytoviruses.
source: The YR proteins encoded by EMALE types 5–8 formed a monophyletic clade and were part of a larger group of recombinases that included virophages from freshwater metagenomes, as well as microalgae and algal nucleocytoviruses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strain BVI had the highest number of virophage elements with 13 complete and 42 partial EMALEs.
source: The four C. burkhardae strains displayed distinct EMALE signatures: strain BVI had the highest number of virophage elements with 13 complete and 42 partial EMALEs, whereas the other three strains had 6–7 complete and 20–22 partial EMALEs each (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Strains Cflag, E4-10, and RCC970 had 6–7 complete and 20–22 partial EMALEs each.
source: The four C. burkhardae strains displayed distinct EMALE signatures: strain BVI had the highest number of virophage elements with 13 complete and 42 partial EMALEs, whereas the other three strains had 6–7 complete and 20–22 partial EMALEs each (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EMALE types 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were present in every host strain.
source: EMALE types 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were present in every host strain, EMALE07 was found in all strains except Cflag, and EMALE types 2 and 8 were detected in strains BVI and E4-10 only.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: EMALE07 was found in all strains except Cflag.
source: EMALE types 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were present in every host strain, EMALE07 was found in all strains except Cflag, and EMALE types 2 and 8 were detected in strains BVI and E4-10 only.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: EMALE types 2 and 8 were detected in strains BVI and E4-10 only.
source: EMALE types 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were present in every host strain, EMALE07 was found in all strains except Cflag, and EMALE types 2 and 8 were detected in strains BVI and E4-10 only.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: There was no evidence for sequence-specific genome integration of EMALEs.
source: We found no evidence for sequence-specific genome integration of EMALEs after inspecting the host DNA sequences that flanked EMALE integration sites, which confirms previous reports of mavirus integration (Fischer and Hackl, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of flanking sequences and citation.

claim: EMALEs were flanked by target site duplications (TSDs) that were predominantly 3–5 bp in length.
source: EMALEs were flanked by target site duplications (TSDs) that were predominantly 3–5 bp in length, although some were as short as 1 bp or as long as 9 bp (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: Mavirus and MPEs generate 5–6 bp long TSDs upon integration.
source: By comparison, mavirus and MPEs generate 5–6 bp long TSDs upon integration (Fischer and Hackl, 2016; Pritham et al., 2007; Kapitonov and Jurka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In 11 cases, an EMALE insertion was conserved in at least two host strains.
source: We found varying degrees of conservation, with examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. In 11 cases, an EMALE insertion was conserved in at least two host strains (Supplementary file 1): three EMALE loci were shared by all four strains, four were shared by three strains, and another four were shared by two strains.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Three EMALE loci were shared by all four strains.
source: We found varying degrees of conservation, with examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. In 11 cases, an EMALE insertion was conserved in at least two host strains (Supplementary file 1): three EMALE loci were shared by all four strains, four were shared by three strains, and another four were shared by two strains.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Four EMALE loci were shared by three strains.
source: We found varying degrees of conservation, with examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. In 11 cases, an EMALE insertion was conserved in at least two host strains (Supplementary file 1): three EMALE loci were shared by all four strains, four were shared by three strains, and another four were shared by two strains.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Four EMALE loci were shared by two strains.
source: We found varying degrees of conservation, with examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. In 11 cases, an EMALE insertion was conserved in at least two host strains (Supplementary file 1): three EMALE loci were shared by all four strains, four were shared by three strains, and another four were shared by two strains.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Strains Cflag and RCC970 were most closely related with nine shared EMALE integrations.
source: Based on conserved EMALE loci, strains Cflag and RCC970 were most closely related with nine shared EMALE integrations, which is in line with phylogenetic and average nucleotide identity (ANI) analyses of these strains (Hackl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis and citation.

claim: The four C. burkhardae genomes have ANIs of >99%.
source: The four C. burkhardae genomes have ANIs of >99% and thus appear to differ mostly based on their content of EMALEs and other MGEs.
evidence: This is supported by ANI analysis.

claim: The four C. burkhardae genomes appear to differ mostly based on their content of EMALEs and other MGEs.
source: The four C. burkhardae genomes have ANIs of >99% and thus appear to differ mostly based on their content of EMALEs and other MGEs.
evidence: This is inferred from the high ANI and observed differences in EMALE content.

claim: 18 of the 33 complete EMALEs represent integrations that were unique to a single host strain.
source: These elements may thus derive from relatively ancient integration events, whereas 18 of the 33 complete EMALEs represent integrations that were unique to a single host strain (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Strain BVI contained 10 unique EMALE integrations, more than twice as many as any other strain.
source: Strain BVI contained 10 of these 18 unique integrations, more than twice as many as any other strain.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Of the 29 different integration sites represented by the 33 fully resolved EMALEs, 18 were located near repetitive host DNA.
source: The genomic landscape around EMALE integration sites ranged from repeat-free flanking regions to complex host repeats (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). Of the 29 different integration sites represented by the 33 fully resolved EMALEs, 18 were located near repetitive host DNA (within 10 kb from the insertion site).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of flanking sequences.

claim: Fifteen EMALE integration sites were located within a predicted host gene.
source: Next, we analyzed whether EMALE insertions interrupted coding sequences of the host. Fifteen integration sites were located within a predicted host gene (13 in exons, 2 in introns), four were found in predicted 3' untranslated regions, and three were located in intergenic regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites relative to host genes.

claim: EMALE insertions may disrupt eukaryotic genes with potential negative consequences for the host.
source: These data show that EMALE insertions may disrupt eukaryotic genes with potential negative consequences for the host.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many EMALEs are inserted in coding sequences.

claim: The apparent preference for integration in coding regions could be assembly related, driven by increased accessibility of euchromatin, or linked to host factors that could direct the rve-INT via its CHROMO domain.
source: The apparent preference for integration in coding regions could be assembly related, driven by increased accessibility of euchromatin, or linked to host factors that could direct the rve-INT via its CHROMO domain (Gao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed integration pattern, with citation.

claim: All EMALE types except EMALE08 should be autonomous for virion formation.
source: With the exception of EMALE08 and EMALE02, all endogenous Cafeteria virophages encode the canonical morphogenesis gene module consisting of MCP, PEN, ATPase, PRO, as well as MV14. EMALE02 likely encodes more distantly related capsid genes. Therefore, all EMALE types except EMALE08 should be autonomous for virion formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of morphogenesis genes.

claim: All EMALEs contain at least one predicted enzyme for genome integration.
source: In addition, all EMALEs contain at least one predicted enzyme for genome integration, an rve-INT in EMALE types 1–7 and a YR in EMALE types 5–8.
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation.

claim: EMALEs encode the enzymatic repertoire for colonizing new host genomes.
source: EMALEs thus encode the enzymatic repertoire for colonizing new host genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of integrase genes.

claim: The high variability of EMALE integration loci among otherwise closely related host strains strongly argues for ongoing colonization of natural Cafeteria populations by virophages.
source: Finally, the high variability of EMALE integration loci among otherwise closely related host strains strongly argues for ongoing colonization of natural Cafeteria populations by virophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: EMALEs may depend on a giant virus for activation and horizontal transmission.
source: The genomic similarity to mavirus implies that EMALEs may also depend on a giant virus for activation and horizontal transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from similarity to mavirus.

claim: The molecular basis of virophage activation lies in the recognition of virophage gene promoters by giant virus encoded transcription factors.
source: Shared regulatory sequences in virophages and their respective giant viruses suggest that the molecular basis of virophage activation lies in the recognition of virophage gene promoters by giant virus encoded transcription factors (Fischer and Suttle, 2011; Claverie and Abergel, 2009; Legendre et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For all type 4 EMALEs, the previously described mavirus promotor motif 'TCTA' was recovered.
source: For all type 4 EMALEs, which include mavirus, we recovered the previously described mavirus promotor motif 'TCTA', flanked by AT-rich regions.
evidence: This is supported by promoter motif analysis.

claim: The 'TCTA' motif corresponds to the conserved late gene promoter in CroV.
source: This motif corresponds to the conserved late gene promoter in CroV (Fischer and Suttle, 2011; Fischer et al., 2010), thus possibly indicating that all type 4 EMALEs could be reactivated by CroV or close relatives.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: All type 4 EMALEs could possibly be reactivated by CroV or close relatives.
source: This motif corresponds to the conserved late gene promoter in CroV (Fischer and Suttle, 2011; Fischer et al., 2010), thus possibly indicating that all type 4 EMALEs could be reactivated by CroV or close relatives.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the presence of the CroV promoter motif.

claim: EMALEs of other types lacked the 'TCTA' motif, but contained putative promoter sequences that may be compatible with different giant viruses.
source: EMALEs of other types lacked the 'TCTA' motif, but contained putative promoter sequences that may be compatible with different giant viruses (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Among the 33 fully resolved EMALEs are three truncated elements.
source: MGEs are prone to various decay processes including pseudogenization, recombination, and truncation. Among the 33 fully resolved EMALEs are three truncated elements: Cflag_215 and RCC970_122 (both EMALE04), and BVI_005 (EMALE08) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in figures.

claim: Even truncated EMALEs are flanked by TIRs, which must have regenerated after the truncation event.
source: Interestingly, even these shorter elements are flanked by TIRs, which must have regenerated after the truncation event.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of TIRs on truncated elements.

claim: The Illumina/PacBio assemblies contained several substitutions and indels compared to Sanger assemblies.
source: To test whether premature stop codons may be the result of assembly artifacts, we amplified selected EMALEs by PCR and analyzed the products using Sanger sequencing. When we compared the Sanger assemblies with the Illumina/PacBio assemblies, we noticed that the latter contained several substitutions and indels.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of sequencing methods.

claim: None of the Sanger assemblies confirmed fragmentation of conserved virophage genes.
source: None of the Sanger assemblies confirmed fragmentation of conserved virophage genes, emphasizing the importance of independent sequence validation.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing validation.

claim: Overall, EMALE ORFs appeared to be intact and are thus likely to encode functional proteins.
source: Overall, EMALE ORFs appeared to be intact and are thus likely to encode functional proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the validation of gene integrity.

claim: About one in four virophage elements was interrupted by a GC-rich sequence with a typical length of ~6 kb.
source: Strikingly, about one in four virophage elements was interrupted by a GC-rich sequence with a typical length of ~6 kb (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The GC-rich insertions in EMALEs were identified as retrotransposons of the Ngaro superfamily, within the DIRS order of retrotransposons.
source: We identified these insertions as retrotransposons of the Ngaro superfamily, within the DIRS order of retrotransposons (Wicker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citation.

claim: Ngaro retrotransposons feature split direct repeats with A1–[ORFs]–B1A2B2 structure.
source: Ngaro retrotransposons feature split direct repeats with A1–[ORFs]–B1A2B2 structure (Figure 5D), encode a YR instead of the rve-INT that is typical for retrotransposons, and are found in various eukaryotes from protists to vertebrates (Poulter and Goodwin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation.

claim: Ngaro retrotransposons encode a YR instead of the rve-INT that is typical for retrotransposons.
source: Ngaro retrotransposons feature split direct repeats with A1–[ORFs]–B1A2B2 structure (Figure 5D), encode a YR instead of the rve-INT that is typical for retrotransposons, and are found in various eukaryotes from protists to vertebrates (Poulter and Goodwin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and citation.

claim: Ngaro retrotransposons are found in various eukaryotes from protists to vertebrates.
source: Ngaro retrotransposons feature split direct repeats with A1–[ORFs]–B1A2B2 structure (Figure 5D), encode a YR instead of the rve-INT that is typical for retrotransposons, and are found in various eukaryotes from protists to vertebrates (Poulter and Goodwin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the four C. burkhardae strains, 80 Ngaro elements were annotated, with 10–25 copies per strain.
source: In the four C. burkhardae strains, we annotated 80 Ngaro elements, with 10–25 copies per strain (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic annotation.

claim: Isolated AB repeats scattered throughout the genome could have arisen from recombination of 5' and 3' repeats.
source: In addition, we found isolated AB repeats scattered throughout the genome, which could have arisen from recombination of 5' and 3' repeats and are reminiscent of solo long terminal repeats of endogenous retroviruses (Friedli and Trono, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of isolated repeats and supported by citation.

claim: Dot plot analysis of concatenated Cafeteria Ngaro sequences revealed four distinct types.
source: Dot plot analysis of concatenated Cafeteria Ngaro sequences revealed four distinct types that showed no similarity at the nucleotide level, but appeared to share the same coding potential (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The four Ngaro types showed no similarity at the nucleotide level, but appeared to share the same coding potential.
source: Dot plot analysis of concatenated Cafeteria Ngaro sequences revealed four distinct types that showed no similarity at the nucleotide level, but appeared to share the same coding potential (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is supported by dot plot and gene annotation analyses.

claim: Ngaro ORF1 may encode a Gag-like protein.
source: Based on synteny to previously described Ngaros, ORF1 may encode a Gag-like protein; ORF2 encodes predicted reverse transcriptase (Pfam PF00078) and ribonuclease H domains (Pfam PF17919); and ORF3 encodes a predicted YR (Pfam PF00589) with the conserved His-X-X-Arg motif and catalytic Tyr residue.
evidence: This is inferred from synteny to previously described Ngaros.

claim: Ngaro ORF2 encodes predicted reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H domains.
source: Based on synteny to previously described Ngaros, ORF1 may encode a Gag-like protein; ORF2 encodes predicted reverse transcriptase (Pfam PF00078) and ribonuclease H domains (Pfam PF17919); and ORF3 encodes a predicted YR (Pfam PF00589) with the conserved His-X-X-Arg motif and catalytic Tyr residue.
evidence: This is supported by domain prediction.

claim: Ngaro ORF3 encodes a predicted YR with the conserved His-X-X-Arg motif and catalytic Tyr residue.
source: Based on synteny to previously described Ngaros, ORF1 may encode a Gag-like protein; ORF2 encodes predicted reverse transcriptase (Pfam PF00078) and ribonuclease H domains (Pfam PF17919); and ORF3 encodes a predicted YR (Pfam PF00589) with the conserved His-X-X-Arg motif and catalytic Tyr residue.
evidence: This is supported by domain prediction.

claim: Ngaro YRs are related to putative transposons of bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: Ngaro YRs are related to putative transposons of bacteria and eukaryotes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but bear no sequence similarity to the EMALE-encoded YRs.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ngaro YRs bear no sequence similarity to the EMALE-encoded YRs.
source: Ngaro YRs are related to putative transposons of bacteria and eukaryotes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but bear no sequence similarity to the EMALE-encoded YRs.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison.

claim: The four Ngaro types in C. burkhardae differed with regard to their integration site preference.
source: Interestingly, the four Ngaro types in C. burkhardae differed with regard to their integration site preference.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: 91% of type 1 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE.
source: Whereas 91% of type 1 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE, this was the case for only 14% and 8% of type 3 and type 4 Ngaros, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: Only 14% of type 3 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE.
source: Whereas 91% of type 1 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE, this was the case for only 14% and 8% of type 3 and type 4 Ngaros, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: Only 8% of type 4 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE.
source: Whereas 91% of type 1 Ngaros were inserted in an EMALE, this was the case for only 14% and 8% of type 3 and type 4 Ngaros, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: 82% of the full-length type 2a Ngaros were inserted in EMALEs.
source: However, several type 2 Ngaros were truncated at their 5' end, featuring ~2 kb long deletions that covered ORF1. All of these deletion variants, which we designate as type 2b, were located in host DNA, in contrast to 82% of the full-length type 2a Ngaros that were inserted in EMALEs (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All type 2b Ngaros (deletion variants) were located in host DNA.
source: However, several type 2 Ngaros were truncated at their 5' end, featuring ~2 kb long deletions that covered ORF1. All of these deletion variants, which we designate as type 2b, were located in host DNA, in contrast to 82% of the full-length type 2a Ngaros that were inserted in EMALEs (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ORF1 determines the integration site specificity of Ngaro retrotransposons.
source: Similarly, most of the type 1 Ngaros that were inserted into eukaryotic chromatin also lacked ORF1. Hence, it appears that ORF1 determines the integration site specificity of Ngaro retrotransposons.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between ORF1 presence and integration site preference.

claim: There was no observed preference of host-genome-integrated Ngaros for regions with a GC-content lower than the host average.
source: We did not observe any preference of host-genome-integrated Ngaros for regions with a GC-content lower than the host average.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites.

claim: There is a significant bias toward Ngaro integration in intergenic EMALE DNA.
source: Out of 20 Ngaro insertion sites with analyzable EMALE flanking regions (including partial EMALEs), 9 were located in intergenic regions, 7 in EMALE genes (1× primase/helicase, 1× pPolB, 1× MV12, 4× MV19), and 4 in TIRs (Supplementary file 1). Considering that intergenic regions comprise only 5–10% of an EMALE genome, we notice a significant bias (p < 1e–5, Fisher's exact test) toward Ngaro integration in intergenic EMALE DNA, which may be caused either by purifying selection of deleterious Ngaro insertions or by a higher preference for Ngaro integration into EMALE intergenic regions, e.g. due to their lower GC-content.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of integration sites.

claim: Ngaro-containing EMALEs did not contain more fragmented genes than Ngaro-free EMALEs.
source: A possible consequence of retrotransposon insertion is the loss of biological activity and subsequent pseudogenization. However, we found that Ngaro-containing EMALEs did not contain more fragmented genes than Ngaro-free EMALEs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Endogenous virophage genomes are abundant and diverse in the marine heterotrophic protist C. burkhardae.
source: In conclusion, we show that endogenous virophage genomes are abundant and diverse in the marine heterotrophic protist C. burkhardae.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by all the genomic data presented.

claim: Mavirus-like EVEs appear to be active and dynamic MGEs with significant potential to shape the genome evolution of their hosts.
